```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd() / "src"))
from lectures import plotting, datasets
from lectures.plotting import INK, COOL, WARM, CRASH, BAND, despine
plotting.set_style("notes")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
R = datasets.load_returns()
meta = datasets.load_basket_meta().set_index("ticker")
BANKS = ["JPM", "BAC", "C", "WFC", "GS"]
```

Two questions run through the rest of the course.  *How bad is a bad day?* —
answered by **Value at Risk**.  *How much of a name's move is just "the market"?*
— answered by the **market factor** and **beta**.  Both are read straight off the
basket here, so the later [VaR](../uncertainty/labs/lab-jobB-portfolio-var.qmd) and
[beta-neutral](../fairness/labs/lab-jobC-beta-neutral.qmd) labs rest on data you've
already seen.

---

## 1 · Value at Risk: a Quantile of the Loss

**Value at Risk (VaR)** at the 5% level is simply the 5th-percentile return: a loss
you expect to *exceed* on only 1 day in 20.  It is the left-tail cutoff from the
crashes page, now given a number.

```{python}
#| label: fig-var
#| fig-cap: "JPM return histogram with the 5% VaR cutoff (the calm-day peak is clipped so the tail stays legible). The shaded region to the cutoff's left is the worst 5% of days; the cutoff itself, about -3.2%, is the daily 5% VaR — the loss exceeded roughly once every 20 trading days."
r = R["JPM"].to_numpy()
var5 = np.quantile(r, 0.05)
peak_days = int(np.histogram(r, bins=70)[0].max())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 4.2))
ax.hist(r, bins=70, color=BAND, alpha=0.85)
ax.axvspan(r.min(), var5, color=CRASH, alpha=0.18, label="worst 5% of days")
ax.axvline(var5, color=CRASH, lw=2)
ax.set_ylim(0, 300)        # cap so the tail + cutoff read; the calm-day peak,
                           # far taller, is clipped and annotated instead
ax.annotate(f"5% VaR = {var5:.1%}", (var5, 250),
            textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-10, 0), ha="right",
            fontsize=10, color=INK)
ax.annotate(f"↑ calm-day peak ≈ {peak_days:,} days", (0.004, 293),
            fontsize=8, color="#666", ha="left", va="top")
ax.set_xlabel("JPM daily log-return"); ax.set_ylabel("days")
ax.set_title("VaR is the left-tail cutoff", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper right"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## VaR Is Not the Worst Case
VaR is the *threshold* of the tail, not its depth.  Days beyond it (the shaded
region) can be far worse — which is exactly why fat tails matter and why the
[uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd) chapter stress-tests it.
:::

## 2 · Diversification, in One Number

Spread the bet across all 14 names (equal weight) and the VaR shrinks: independent
wobbles partly cancel.  But spread it across the five **banks** only and you get
almost no relief — they co-crash (previous page), so a five-bank basket is barely
safer than a single bank.

```{python}
#| label: fig-port-var
#| fig-cap: "5% daily VaR for single names vs portfolios. The diversified 14-name portfolio cuts the tail to about -2.0%; a banks-only portfolio stays near -3.2% — no better than holding JPM alone — because the banks fall together. Diversification only helps where co-movement is low."
mkt = R.mean(axis=1)                       # equal-weight all 14
bankport = R[BANKS].mean(axis=1)
items = {
    "JPM (single)": R["JPM"], "BAC (single)": R["BAC"],
    "Banks portfolio": bankport, "All-14 portfolio": mkt,
}
vals = {k: np.quantile(v, 0.05) * 100 for k, v in items.items()}
colors = [COOL, COOL, CRASH, plotting.PALETTE["green"]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 3.8))
ax.barh(list(vals.keys()), list(vals.values()), color=colors)
ax.set_xlabel("5% daily VaR (%)")
ax.set_title("Diversification helps — unless everything co-crashes", fontsize=12)
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## 3 · The Market Factor and Beta

Most of any stock's daily move is just the **market** moving.  Proxy the market by
the equal-weight average return, then **beta** is the slope of a stock's return
regressed on it: $\beta = \mathrm{cov}(r, m) / \mathrm{var}(m)$.  $\beta > 1$ means
the name amplifies the market; $\beta < 1$ means it dampens it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-beta-scatter
#| fig-cap: "JPM return vs the equal-weight market factor, with the regression line. The slope is JPM's beta, about 1.42: a 1% market day moves JPM ~1.4% on average. The tight scatter shows how much of JPM is simply 'the market'."
m = mkt.to_numpy()
y = R["JPM"].to_numpy()
beta = np.cov(y, m)[0, 1] / np.var(m)
xs = np.linspace(m.min(), m.max(), 100)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.4))
ax.scatter(m, y, s=9, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
ax.plot(xs, beta * xs + (y.mean() - beta * m.mean()), color=CRASH, lw=2.4,
        label=f"beta = {beta:.2f}")
ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.6); ax.axvline(0, color=INK, lw=0.6)
ax.set_xlabel("market factor return (equal-weight)")
ax.set_ylabel("JPM return")
ax.set_title("Beta is the slope on the market", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Compute it for the whole basket and the sector story returns once more: banks
amplify the market (high beta), utilities and staples cushion it (low beta).

```{python}
#| label: fig-beta-bars
#| fig-cap: "Market beta by name. Banks (red) lead at 1.3–1.85; defensive utilities and staples (green) sit near 0.45–0.5. Beta and volatility tell the same ranking from two angles."
betas = (pd.Series({t: np.cov(R[t], mkt)[0, 1] / np.var(mkt) for t in R.columns})
         .sort_values())
colors = [CRASH if meta.loc[t, "sector"] == "Banks"
          else plotting.PALETTE["green"]
          if meta.loc[t, "sector"] in ("Utilities", "Staples")
          else COOL for t in betas.index]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2))
ax.barh(betas.index, betas.values, color=colors)
ax.axvline(1.0, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="market (beta = 1)")
ax.set_xlabel("beta to the market factor")
ax.set_title("Banks amplify the market; defensives cushion it", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="lower right"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Bridge to Fairness
"Beta-neutral" means a strategy whose returns don't load on the market factor —
$\beta \approx 0$.  That is *identical* to "fair": a prediction that doesn't load
on a protected attribute.  The [fairness](../fairness/index.qmd) module makes this
exact, swapping the market factor for `sex`.
:::
